name: Nora Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've been on the water billing phones for fourteen years. A caller reads the meter, I compare it with the last bill, then I explain why the balance is what it is. I finished secondary school, and I know the ordinary cases well, though the strange account faults still send me to a colleague.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what makes a shift difficult?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like telling a worried customer exactly which payment was missed, without making them feel foolish. The company has an AI helper, but I never use it; I keep a paper list of account numbers while I work. My husband Leon is a school caretaker, our daughter lives in her own flat, and we have roughly three months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that small shortcuts are not a reason to stop reading the meter number aloud. People have waited half an hour to speak to us, and customers need a correction with a named meter reading. A tidy summary is no answer if the water bill is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the billing line to carry on, so my wage should stay. Even so, a boiler repair could eat our three-month reserve, and Leon's school wage pays only part of the household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking the meter reading against the previous bill and write down any repeat wrong balances. In the first year of AI Plateau, I would ask the supervisor to keep enough paid time for that check, and Leon and I would postpone replacing our working dining table until the reserve is stronger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money we already owe, not frightened by this small change. I can keep doing the job I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of error would a shortcut miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a caller was sent three corrected bills, and each one repeated the same wrong reading. A little software speed would not have spotted the entry unless somebody checked the meter number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our daughter has rent to pay and should not become our repair fund. We can wait on a table; we cannot wait on a broken boiler.

say: I would tell colleagues **meter readings** still need a person's check.
I would say a **neat summary** cannot fix a wrong bill.
think: I expect my **billing wage** to continue in a mild change.
I worry a **boiler repair** could use much of our three-month reserve.
do: Keep checking **meter readings** and record repeat wrong balances.
Postpone the **dining table** replacement while Leon and I strengthen our reserve.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about repair costs, while the job itself looks stable.
S0.quote: A tidy summary is no answer if the water bill is wrong.
fieldNote: She **never uses AI** and relies on meter and account records.
Potential **boiler repair costs** and the limits of three months saved worry her more than a mild software change.

steps.text: Keep checking water meter readings against previous bills and record repeat wrong balances
Postpone replacing the working dining table while the three-month reserve grows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the water team to ask which paid calls are left, not celebrate that the computer answers quickly. The straightforward balance questions are a large part of our day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experience helps with the odd accounts, but I am not the fastest with new screens. If the ordinary calls go, the company may keep fewer agents and I could lose paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep a weekly tally of wrong balances that need a person and ask our supervisor for the proposed billing rota in writing. If my hours fall in the first year routine calls move, I would check advertised water and utility desks nearby, but I would keep my current shifts until a written paid offer covered our rent and the bus journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious because the familiar queue could shrink before I learn a new one. I can ask for the figures without pretending I like the helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which calls would you tally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count calls where the customer asks us to explain an old payment, not just the first balance question. Those are the ones that take ten minutes, and someone still has to answer them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a nearby desk solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might look at the nearby electricity desk, but its hours might be limited. A short rota at another utility desk is no rescue for our rent. Leon and I would compare the whole week's paid hours with rent and travel before I signed anything.

say: I would ask what **paid calls** remain when balance questions move to software.
I would tell colleagues **old-payment disputes** still need human explanation.
think: I may lose **paid billing hours** despite my experience with odd accounts.
I am **slow on new screens**, so another desk is uncertain.
do: Tally **wrong balances** and ask for the proposed billing rota in writing.
Check **advertised utility desks** after cuts; keep current shifts until rent-and-bus-covering written work exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller paid week.
S1.quote: A short rota at another utility desk is no rescue for our rent.
fieldNote: Her **ordinary balance queue** is exposed despite years of experience.
She tests **whole-week pay**, rent and bus costs before changing desks or leaving paid billing shifts.

steps.text: Keep tallying human billing disputes and ask for the paid billing rota in writing
If hours fall, check advertised nearby utility jobs with full-week pay covering rent and bus fare
Keep current water-billing shifts until a suitable written paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the 2028 date puts the billing phones directly in the way, since a thinking system can answer most account questions. Repairs and other hands-on work face robots later, around 2031, but that does not keep my wages coming now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company could cut most of my shifts before I find another desk. Three months of savings and Leon's school wage would not carry the rent for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask payroll for my last six wage slips and list the rent, heating and food bills with Leon. If the phone rota collapses in the first year after 2028, I would ask the school about any posted paid office cover and check its actual hours; I would not leave remaining paid calls unless the weekly money after travel covered our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; I can picture the call queue going quiet while rent still comes due. The list of bills gives us a starting point, but it does not create work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Leon know of a school opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am not assuming the school has a place because Leon works there. He can ask whether an opening is posted, and I would apply in the usual way if the pay and hours are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the rent is late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can come round for tea, but she is paying for her own flat. I would ask the landlord about a payment schedule if we actually missed a rent date, rather than promise family money we don't have.

say: I would warn that **2028 thinking AI** reaches billing before repair robots.
I would say **school work** is an option only if a paid opening is posted.
think: I expect **most phone shifts** could end quickly.
I cannot cover **rent for long** from three months saved and Leon's wage.
do: Gather **six wage slips** and list household bills with Leon in 2026.
Check **posted paid school cover** if the 2028 rota collapses; retain calls until after-travel weekly pay covers bills.
Ask the landlord for a **payment schedule** only if we actually miss a rent date.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely major hours loss.
S2.quote: The list of bills gives us a starting point, but it does not create work.
fieldNote: She does not mistake **Leon's school job** for a guaranteed opening.
A **rent gap** could arise quickly if her own rota collapses despite Leon keeping his caretaker wage.

steps.text: Keep paid billing shifts and obtain six wage slips to list bills with Leon
If the 2028 rota collapses, ask about posted paid school office cover and check hours
Take school cover only with after-travel weekly pay covering bills; retain paid calls until then
If rent is actually missed, ask the landlord about a payment schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my neighbours the 2031 date gives us some time, but the call desk still meets thinking AI first. Robots may reach hands-on repairs around 2034, and that is a separate worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be 63 with a little more saved, though nothing says our income would replace wages then. I would rather learn the council's paper-and-screen appointment desk than gamble on a course advertised for a job nobody posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the local council desk whether it posts paid part-time appointment work and what a normal shift actually involves. I would keep taking water calls and set aside the money from one extra paid Saturday each month if the centre offers it; in the first year after 2031 I would apply only if a paid council vacancy exists with hours that cover our bills after bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have time to ask a person what happens at the desk. I can take the bus there and ask at the public counter. A course for a job nobody posted is a bill, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the council desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether that job means handling visitors as well as typing forms. If it is all forms on a screen, the new AI may remove it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I might want fewer hours by then, but Leon and I have not checked what income could replace either wage. I would read the actual statements before treating 63 as a stopping date.

say: I would say **2031 AGI** changes desk work before 2034 robots reach repairs.
I would ask about **real council shifts**, not buy a course without a job.
think: I might save a little more by **age 63** if extra paid shifts exist.
I cannot assume an **income after work** that Leon and I have not checked.
do: Ask the **council desk** what posted paid appointment shifts involve.
Keep **water calls** and save one offered Saturday's pay monthly.
Apply after 2031 only for **posted paid council work** with bill-covering weekly hours and wages after bus fare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about desk jobs, while time permits a careful enquiry.
S3.quote: A course for a job nobody posted is a bill, not a plan.
fieldNote: She prefers a **face-to-face enquiry** over a speculative course.
An offered **Saturday shift** could build savings, while any 2031 move needs posted bill-covering hours after bus fare.

steps.text: Keep taking water calls and ask the council about actual paid appointment duties
Save pay from one extra Saturday monthly only if the centre offers that shift
After 2031, apply for posted paid council work with after-bus-fare weekly hours and wages covering bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my family that a ten-year warning is useful only while we are still paid to use it. Thinking AI could change our billing desk by 2036, with hands-on robots about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still need paid work, depending on our actual income and bills. I have no right to declare that Leon and I can live on savings because three months of expenses is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 we would put our actual income and savings statements on the kitchen table and compare them with a full year of bills. I would keep my paid billing shifts and ask each autumn for the next year's rota; in the first year after 2036, I would keep working if the verified money falls short and look only at real offered hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, since I have ten years to get the numbers straight. I do not think a date in a story pays a rent bill. Three months of expenses saved is not a wage at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask payroll?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask payroll what hours are actually being offered, not whether the company hopes to keep a human desk. I know what a promise sounds like after fourteen years on the phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter fill a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon and I would look at the written figures together, but we will not budget our daughter's wage. She pays for her own flat, and I would rather tell her honestly if we need to keep working.

say: I would tell family a **ten-year warning** is useful only with continuing pay.
I would say **2036 billing AI** comes before 2039 repair robots.
think: I may still **need wages at 68** if verified income cannot meet bills.
I cannot treat **three months saved** as a full replacement wage.
do: Compare **actual statements** with a full year of bills in 2026.
Keep **paid billing shifts** and request each autumn's rota; continue after 2036 if income falls short.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later income, though the decade gives time to check.
S4.quote: Three months of expenses saved is not a wage at 68.
fieldNote: She insists on **written hours** and verified income before reducing work.
Her daughter's **own rent** rules out treating family wages as guaranteed support when planning work at 68.

steps.text: Keep paid water-billing shifts and request the next year's rota each autumn
Compare actual income and savings statements while continuing paid shifts
Continue paid work after 2036 if verified household income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I can picture the phones going before I find another paid week. A written rota, a real opening and time to discuss the bills with Leon would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the new job gets me home on the last bus. A wage on paper is no good if I cannot reach the shift.

headlineQuote: A wage on paper is no good if I cannot reach the shift.
portrait: A **58-year-old** water-billing agent with secondary-school education and fourteen years' ordinary experience.
She **never uses AI**, preferring meter records and paper account notes.
Her husband is a **school caretaker**; their grown daughter has her own rent.
She has about **three months saved** and tests offers against full-week pay and transport.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could remove most billing shifts before another paid week appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **written rota**, a genuine paid opening and time to compare bills with Leon would help.
